newsitem.title: USA: Albright hints Argentina to be non-NATO U.S. ally.
newsitem.headline: Albright hints Argentina to be non-NATO U.S. ally.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Wednesday that the United States was likely to grant Argentina status as a major non-NATO ally.
"The announcement has not yet been made but we do wish to recognize Argentina's role," she told reporters.
The designation would put Argentina in the same category as Israel, Egypt, Japan, South Korea and Jordan.
"This is a status that is not a security relationship," she said.

"It does not provide fighter planes or anything like that. It is basically a relationship that recognizes symbolically a country's relationship with the United States and it's open to other countries including Chile," she said.
Albright made her comments during a picture-taking session with Chilean Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza.
Argentina urged the top U.S. military officer, Gen. John Shalikashvili, to grant it major non-NATO ally status when he visited Buenos Aires in July.

President Carlos Menem has been eager for the designation in recognition for making Argentina one of the strongest U.S,. allies in South America, for its military support role in the 1991 Gulf War and its role in international peacekeeping from Croatia to Cyprus and Haiti.
Albright specifically cited the fact that Argentina has been "an important contributor to peace-keeping operations with the United Nations."
Argentina, which has ended conscription and slashed defense spending since its return to democracy in 1983, is keen to parlay the status so that American-made war materiel is easier to acquire.
While the status would not improve Argentina's access to advanced weaponry, it would allow the country to buy on a priority basis such excess items as ammunition and spare parts from the Pentagon.
However, President Bill Clinton on Aug. 1 gave all countries in Latin America a huge boost when he lifted an effective 20-year ban on the sale of U.S.-made advanced weapons to the region.

U.S. officials say Chile is nearest to taking advantage of that new arms policy. The country is considering purchasing advanced fighter aircraft and could make a decision by year's end. Major U.S. producers, as well as some Europeans, are competing for the contract.
Clinton is scheduled to visit Argentina and Brazil in October.
